title: Path Sum II
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting every path then filtering afterward versus DFS with backtracking and incremental sum tracking.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of the node values along the path equals targetSum exactly.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root, targetSum"],["Output","All root-to-leaf paths (as value lists) summing exactly to targetSum"],["Goal","DFS with backtracking, tracking the running path and remaining sum needed"],["Constraints","Up to 5000 nodes"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"All root-to-leaf paths matching a condition\"","DFS with backtracking: build a path incrementally, check the condition at each leaf, and undo (backtrack) the choice before trying the next branch"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Every valid answer must be a complete root-to-leaf path (ending exactly at a node with no children), whose values sum to targetSum. Since a path can only be confirmed valid once a leaf is reached, this naturally calls for a depth-first search that maintains the CURRENT path so far and the remaining sum still needed, checking the condition only at leaves.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Delivery Routes That Add Up to an Exact Total Distance
blocks.text: Picture exploring every possible delivery route from a depot down to each final stop, keeping a running tally of remaining distance needed; only when a route reaches its actual final stop (a leaf) does it make sense to check whether the tally hit exactly zero.

blocks.caption: DFS tracking the current path and remaining sum; at a leaf, remaining sum reaching zero means a valid path

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: tree = [5, 4, 8, 11, null, 13, 4, 7, 2, null, null, 5, 1], targetSum = 22
Result: [[5,4,11,2],[5,8,4,5]]. Path 5-4-11-2 sums to 22, and path 5-8-4-5 also sums to 22.
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A valid answer must be a COMPLETE root-to-leaf path, so the check for "does this sum to targetSum" can only be made once a leaf is actually reached.

Observation 2: Maintaining a running "remaining sum needed" (starting at targetSum, subtracting each node's value as it is visited) means a leaf with exactly zero remaining sum is precisely a valid path.

Observation 3: Building the current path incrementally as a shared list (pushing the current node's value before recursing into children, popping it off after returning) lets the SAME list be reused across the whole search, avoiding constructing a fresh list for every branch.

Observation 4: Only when a valid path is found at a leaf does a COPY of the current path need to be saved into the results, since the shared list continues to change as the search backtracks and explores other branches.
This leads to a DFS with backtracking, maintaining a shared path list and a running remaining sum, saving a copy of the path whenever a leaf is reached with exactly zero remaining.
6. Brute Force Solution
Enumerate every complete root-to-leaf path first (regardless of its sum), then filter afterward to keep only the ones summing to targetSum.
Why the code is written this way

items: Collecting every path first, then filtering afterward, implements the two ideas (find paths, check sum) as separate clear steps.
This computes each path's sum in a separate pass after the fact, when the sum can just as easily be tracked incrementally during the same DFS that builds the path.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case, storing every path then summing each afterward.
Space: O(n squared) worst case for storing every complete path.
Limitation: tracking the remaining sum incrementally during the SAME DFS that builds the path avoids a separate summing pass, and only actually valid paths get copied into the results.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain a shared path list and a "remaining sum needed" value, starting at targetSum. During DFS: push the current node's value onto the path, subtract it from the remaining sum. If this is a leaf AND the remaining sum is now exactly zero, save a COPY of the current path into the results. Otherwise, recurse into the left and right children with the updated remaining sum. After returning from both children, pop the current node's value off the shared path (backtracking), so sibling branches see the correct path state.
Use DFS with backtracking, tracking remaining sum incrementally and checking the condition directly at each leaf.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for path 5-4-11-2, targetSum = 22

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node visited","Remaining sum after subtracting"],"rows":[["5","17"],["4","13"],["11","2"],["2 (leaf)","0, MATCH: path [5,4,11,2] saved"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Tracking the remaining sum incrementally (subtracting each node's value as it is visited) is equivalent to computing the path's total sum, but spreads that computation across the DFS itself rather than requiring a separate pass; checking the condition exactly at leaves, combined with backtracking (popping the path after exploring both children), correctly and efficiently finds every valid root-to-leaf path without ever re-summing a path from scratch.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case for copying valid paths (each up to O(n) long), but avoids the extra summing pass.
Space: O(h) for the shared path plus recursion depth, plus O(n squared) worst case for the stored results.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Path Sum II is the canonical DFS-with-backtracking-on-trees problem: build a shared path incrementally, check the condition at leaves, and undo choices to explore siblings correctly.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to pop the current node off the shared path list after recursing (forgetting to backtrack), corrupting the path seen by sibling branches.
Saving a reference to the shared path list directly into the results instead of a COPY, which would later show the wrong (backtracked) values.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["No path sums to targetSum","Returns an empty list."],["A path that reaches the target sum at a non-leaf node","Not counted, since the path must end exactly at a leaf."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "check the sum condition only at leaves, and always save a copy, never a reference, of the current path" heads off the two most common bugs in this pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find all root-to-leaf paths matching a condition", think: DFS with backtracking, using a shared path list and undoing choices after each branch.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you solve the simpler variant, Path Sum I, which only needs to check if ANY such path exists (a boolean), not enumerate all of them?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Path Sum and Binary Tree Paths, both closely related DFS-with-backtracking tree problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches cost similarly in the worst case due to path storage; the incremental-sum approach avoids a separate summing pass, integrating the check directly into the DFS.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: DFS with backtracking, using a shared path list and an incrementally tracked remaining sum.
Core Idea: check the sum condition only at leaves; save a copy of the path when it matches; always backtrack (pop) after exploring a branch.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for both approaches, due to path copying.
Space: O(n squared) worst case for the brute force's full path collection, O(h) plus result storage for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: tracking remaining sum incrementally avoids a separate summing pass over each collected path.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, foundational DFS-with-backtracking tree problem.
One line memory trick: track remaining sum as you go, save a copy only at a matching leaf.
